prompt: What does this course ask you to install before lesson 2?
hint: The practice is reading, writing and drawing.

choices.text: A local PostgreSQL and the Carreto monolith
choices.why: Carreto is invented and there is no system to run; its code is described, not shipped.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: a text editor, a way to draw and a spreadsheet are all the course uses, and each has a free option you may already have.

choices.text: Python 3, for the exercises in every lesson
choices.why: Python appears once, in lesson 9, and running it there is optional; reading the program and its output is enough.

choices.text: A paid diagramming tool
choices.why: diagrams.net and Excalidraw are free, and paper and pencil are a full alternative.

prompt: Why does the lesson say paper is not a lesser choice for drawing an architecture?
hint: Think about what a tool tempts you to spend time on.

choices.text: Paper diagrams are easier to keep up to date
choices.why: Paper is harder to update, not easier; the argument is about the act of drawing.

choices.text: Diagram tools hide the connectors between components
choices.why: A tool draws connectors perfectly well; what it encourages is polishing the layout.

choices.text: It forces you to decide what the boxes are
choices.why: Right: deciding what the elements are is the skill, and a tool's alignment and colours pull attention towards neatness.

choices.text: Reviewers trust hand drawings more
choices.why: Trust comes from whether the drawing matches the system, which lesson 2 checks; the medium does not earn it.

prompt: Match each person at Carreto to their role.
hint: The course's table of people.

prompt: In Booch's definition, what makes a design decision "significant" enough to be architecture?
hint: One measure, and it is about the future.

choices.text: How senior the person who made it is
choices.why: Seniority describes who decided, not what the decision costs; a junior's shortcut on a shared table is still architectural.

choices.text: Whether it appears on the high-level diagram
choices.why: A diagram is a view chosen by somebody; the shared loads table was architectural and appeared on none.

choices.text: Its cost of change
choices.why: Right: "where significant is measured by cost of change" — a test you can apply to any decision.

choices.text: How many lines of code implement it
choices.why: The currency precision is a few lines and touches every financial record; size of code is a poor proxy.

prompt: Bass, Clements and Kazman write "the set of structures", in the plural. What does the plural point at?
hint: Carreto's code, its running services and its teams.

choices.text: Module, runtime and allocation views of one system
choices.why: Right: how the code is divided, what runs and talks, and where it runs and who owns it; none alone is the architecture.

choices.text: One structure per service, so fourteen at Carreto
choices.why: The plural is about kinds of structure across the whole system, not a count of deployables.

choices.text: The successive versions of the system over time
choices.why: Evolution matters to the standard's definition, but the plural here names different views of the same system.

choices.text: The diagrams the team keeps in its wiki
choices.why: Diagrams describe structures; the structures exist in the system whether drawn or not.

prompt: Carreto's Driver app is built with one UI framework, and replacing it would take the Driver team months. How does the lesson classify that decision?
hint: Cost of change, and also who pays it.

choices.text: Not architectural, because it is a UI concern
choices.why: Being about screens does not make a decision cheap; months of one team's work is a real cost of change.

choices.text: Architectural for Carreto as a whole, like the loads table
choices.why: The loads table binds three teams; the UI framework touches one, which is why the scopes differ.

choices.text: Architectural for that one application, barely for the company
choices.why: Right: expensive for one team and nearly free for everybody else — the distinction lesson 4 builds into levels.

choices.text: Undecidable until somebody draws it
choices.why: Drawing does not make a decision architectural; the cost of reversing it does, and that cost is known.

prompt: A team stores timestamps in local time without a zone. It is three lines of code, and five services now read those timestamps. Which reading does the lesson support?
hint: Compare it with the currency precision row.

choices.text: Too small to be architectural
choices.why: Small in code says nothing about the data already stored and the five readers; that is the trap the currency row shows.

choices.text: Architectural: cheap in code, expensive in data and readers
choices.why: Right: changing it means fixing stored values and five consumers, which is a high cost of change across teams.

choices.text: Architectural only if the architect made it
choices.why: Who decided does not change what it costs to undo; the shared loads table was nobody's decision.

choices.text: A coding-style issue for a linter to settle
choices.why: A linter can flag the habit, but the stored data and the readers make it a structural problem.

prompt: Johnson's description, reported by Fowler: architecture is about "the ___ stuff, whatever that is".
hint: The word that makes it depend on the system.

prompt: Nobody at Carreto ever decided that three teams would share the loads table. What follows, by the lesson?
hint: Does a system need a decision to have an architecture?

choices.text: It is technical debt, so it is outside the architecture
choices.why: Debt can be architectural; the sharing shapes what fails together and what costs months to change.

choices.text: It does not count until a document records it
choices.why: A document describes the architecture; the shared table is part of it today with no document at all.

choices.text: It was the founders' decision, made in 2017
choices.why: The founders chose one database; the three-team sharing accumulated one query at a time afterwards.

choices.text: It is architecture anyway, arrived at by accumulation
choices.why: Right: a system has an architecture whether or not anybody chose it, and this piece came one query at a time.

prompt: Three services are called in a synchronous chain, each available 99.9% of the time. To one decimal place, what percentage of the time is the whole chain available?
hint: The probabilities multiply.

prompt: With the Shipper app, Pricing and Matching joined by synchronous calls, what happens to shippers when Pricing is down?
hint: Every part has to be up at once.

choices.text: They post loads and see the quote later
choices.why: That is the queue version; in a synchronous chain nothing waits for Pricing to return.

choices.text: They cannot post a load
choices.why: Right: the Shipper app waits on Pricing, so a failure there stops posting, although posting itself is fine.

choices.text: Matching offers loads at the last known price
choices.why: Nothing in the synchronous version keeps a last known price; the call to Pricing fails and the request with it.

choices.text: They notice nothing, since the database is shared
choices.why: There is no shared database in this version; that is the third wiring.

prompt: Pricing consumes "load posted" messages from a queue and is down for 20 minutes while shippers post 30 loads a minute. What is waiting when it returns, and what new duty did the queue create?
hint: Multiply, then think about what grows quietly.

choices.text: 30 messages; tracing every call
choices.why: 30 is one minute of posting, and tracing is the synchronous chain's strength, not the queue's new duty.

choices.text: 600 messages; versioning the API between the services
choices.why: The count is right, but a queue versions a message format, and the duty the lesson names is watching depth.

choices.text: 600 messages; watching the queue's depth
choices.why: Right: 20 × 30 = 600, and a queue that grows unwatched is an outage nobody has noticed yet.

choices.text: None, since messages are lost while Pricing is down
choices.why: A broker keeps messages for consumers that are away; losing them would defeat the point of the queue.

prompt: Why does a diagram of the shared-database version say so little about its coupling?
hint: Look at where the lines go.

choices.text: Databases are drawn smaller than services
choices.why: Size on the page is not the issue; the dependency between the services is simply not drawn.

choices.text: No arrow joins the boxes; each has a line to the database
choices.why: Right: the services depend on each other through the tables, and the drawing shows only three lines down.

choices.text: Shared databases have no coupling to show
choices.why: They have the heaviest coupling of the three: a column change is a change to three teams' code.

choices.text: The coupling lives in the broker's configuration
choices.why: There is no broker in this wiring; the coupling lives in the table definitions and the queries.

prompt: Match each connector to what the person on call sees when it goes wrong.
hint: The last row of the lesson's table.

pairs.right: a slow database and no obvious culprit

prompt: Pricing's team rewrites the inside of Pricing in a quarter and nobody notices. Changing Pricing from a synchronous call to an event consumer touches the Shipper app, its screens, monitoring and the runbook. What does the contrast show?
hint: Elements, relations, and the properties of both.

choices.text: Rewrites are cheaper than people think
choices.why: The rewrite was cheap for outsiders because it stayed behind the connector, which is the point being made.

choices.text: Event consumers are harder to build and to test than HTTP services are
choices.why: Neither is hard to build; the cost lies in everything outside Pricing that depends on how it is reached.

choices.text: Connectors cost more to change than a component's insides
choices.why: Right: that difference is why connectors are architecture and a service's internals frequently are not.

choices.text: Monitoring is part of the component
choices.why: Monitoring is affected because the connector changed; the lesson is about the connector, not where monitoring lives.

prompt: When Renata draws Carreto for the first time, what does she write beside every line?
hint: An unlabelled arrow lets each reader imagine a different one.

choices.text: The team that owns it
choices.why: Ownership matters in the allocation structure, but the label she adds answers what the line is.

choices.text: The date it was added
choices.why: Dates belong on the diagram as a whole, which lesson 2 asks for; each line gets its kind.

choices.text: Its average latency
choices.why: Latency is a measurement that changes daily; the label states a decision that does not.

choices.text: The kind of connector
choices.why: Right: "HTTP, waits for reply", "event via broker", "reads table loads" — three different relations that look identical unlabelled.

prompt: Who, in the lesson's sense, is a stakeholder of Carreto's system?
hint: Affected by it, or able to affect it.

choices.text: The engineers who write its code
choices.why: They are stakeholders, but so are shippers, drivers and the finance director; the definition is wider.

choices.text: Anybody affected by the system or able to affect it
choices.why: Right: shippers, drivers, finance, product and the teams all qualify, and each wants something different.

choices.text: The people who pay for it
choices.why: Payers are one group; drivers and the Platform team pay nothing and are clearly affected.

choices.text: Shareholders of the company
choices.why: In architecture the word is broader than in finance: anybody the structure answers to.

prompt: ANTT's freight floor changes over time. Which requirement does that create for Carreto, by the lesson?
hint: A shipper disputes a quote months later.

choices.text: Quotes must be recalculated whenever the floor changes
choices.why: Old quotes stand as made; the problem is proving they were legal at the time.

choices.text: Pricing has to be merged back into the monolith
choices.why: Where Pricing runs is unrelated; the requirement is about what is kept.

choices.text: Keeping which floor table was in force for each quote
choices.why: Right: a regulatory rule became a data-retention requirement, which shapes what Pricing stores.

choices.text: A faster connection to the tax authority
choices.why: The tax authority authorises CT-e; the floor comes from ANTT and is about what a quote may be.

prompt: How does Carreto's loads table illustrate Conway's law?
hint: Who used to be one team?

choices.text: Tracking got a separate database because it was the first team to be split off
choices.why: Tracking does illustrate the law, but the question is about the loads table.

choices.text: Three teams that were once one still share the old team's table
choices.why: Right: the shared table is the trace the old team's communication structure left in the code.

choices.text: The table is slow because three teams query it
choices.why: Slowness is a symptom of sharing; Conway's law is about structure copying communication.

choices.text: Conway's law requires one table per team
choices.why: It is an observation about what happens, not a rule anybody has to follow.

prompt: A consultant proposes for Carreto an architecture that a company with ten times its platform staff runs well. What does the lesson say about it?
hint: Operations is part of the environment.

choices.text: It is a bad design for Carreto if it needs skill Carreto lacks
choices.why: Right: a design that needs more operational skill than the company has is bad for that company, however well it works elsewhere.

choices.text: It is good, since it is proven at scale
choices.why: Proven somewhere with different staff says little about running it with a small Platform team.

choices.text: Operations is the Platform team's concern, not the architecture's
choices.why: The lesson counts operations as one of the five forces an architecture answers to.

choices.text: It should be adopted and the team hired later
choices.why: Adopting first leaves Carreto running something nobody can repair in the meantime.

prompt: Why does the lesson call quality attributes "what an architecture is for"?
hint: Could posting a load be built on fourteen services? On two hundred?

choices.text: Functional requirements belong to the business analyst and not to the architect
choices.why: Functionality matters to everyone; the point is that structure barely constrains it.

choices.text: They are easier to measure than features
choices.why: Many are harder to measure, which is why lesson 6 teaches how to state them precisely.

choices.text: Almost any structure delivers the features; structures differ in how well
choices.why: Right: speed, reliability, security, cost of change and auditability are what a structure decides.

choices.text: Regulators set them directly
choices.why: Regulation is one source among five; drivers, teams and operations produce them too.

prompt: Match each force in Carreto's environment to the quality attribute it turns into.
hint: The closing paragraphs of section 05.

pairs.left: drivers on a weak mobile signal
the tax authority authorising each CT-e
seven teams changing their own parts

prompt: Renata is asked which of these Carreto decisions are architectural. Using the lesson's tests, choose all that apply.
hint: Cost of change, and who has to agree to change it.

choices.text: Matching reads new loads by polling the monolith's loads table
choices.why: Yes: a shared-table connector binding Matching to the monolith's schema, expensive to change.

choices.text: Payments formats log lines as JSON
choices.why: Cheap to change and inside one team; a library or a setting replaces it in a day.

choices.text: The monolith calls Pricing over HTTP and waits for the quote
choices.why: Yes: a synchronous connector that makes posting depend on Pricing being up.

choices.text: Quotes are stored in reais with two decimal places
choices.why: Yes: small in code, but every stored quote and invoice would have to change.

prompt: Put the steps of a load at Carreto in the order the lesson describes, from the shipper's action to the driver's payment.
hint: The how-this-course-works section describes the flow.
items: The load is offered to suitable drivers
trap: Paying before the delivery is proved would pay for work nobody has confirmed.
